Low voltage high current vehicle battery cables--I coat the stripped wire with rosin, insert in lug, crimp tightly, and then solder. A piece of shrink tubing and I am done. I also use Burndy split bolt connectors when I need to make a splice or 'T' connection. I cover the Burndy with either self-fusing tape or monkey shit, friction tape and then Scotch 33+. Copper welding cable is great for winches--I use 2 gauge for that. Welding cable has a tough high temperature rubber insulation, available in any length and is multi-stranded so it is very flexible. My winch battery is in the boot of my Rubicon Jeep and I use quick disconnects from Warn. I can connect my winch to the front or rear of the Jeep. I have found being able to winch backwards is as useful as winching forwards as I have already gone as far as I can and need to back up for another run at it.

The UL and other codes do not permit 2 wires in 1 lug unless the device is designed for it. It is also not a good idea to use a smaller lug than will fit the wire by cutting and removing strands. The lugs are rated to match the current carrying capacity of the wire. The insulation sleeve on a terminal should not be pierced by the crimping tool but almost every industrial maintenance electrician does it because the mashing type of crimping tool does not always do a gas-tilght seal. Just a few quick notes from years of experience.
